0.1).","printedPage":365,"pdfPage":383,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":31},{"text":"The amount that testosterone increases in an emotional situation .","printedPage":365,"pdfPage":383,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":32},{"text":"Because females start with low testosterone levels, an increase .","printedPage":365,"pdfPage":383,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":34},{"text":"This result fits with other research finding that committees work .","printedPage":365,"pdfPage":383,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":35},{"text":"In all cultures, males are more likely to fight than females, commit .","printedPage":365,"pdfPage":383,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":42},{"text":"Overall, low serotonin turnover does appear to correlate with human .","printedPage":366,"pdfPage":384,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":52},{"text":"The suitability of the startle reflex to measure anxiety means that .","printedPage":368,"pdfPage":386,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":64},{"text":"A control group is tested with a stimulus that was not paired with It is as if the first attack gets the hamster in the mood to fight.","During that period, activity builds up in the corticomedial area of the amygdala (Figure 11.10), and as it does so, it increases the hamster’s probability of attacking.","Some people have argued that it is “in our animal nature” to be violent, at least for males.","troops are extremely, even murderously aggressive, but chimps in other troops are much less aggressive, and bonobos rarely fight at all. People are capable of unspeakable cruelty, but cooperative behavior is vastly more common.","Twin studies generally indicate significant heritability, but the results vary for many reasons, including how the researchers measure aggression.","A study of prisoners with a history of extreme impulsive violence found that 123 of the 281 men studied had one or more rare genetic variants linked to brain functioning.","Of the rare genetic variants linked to a high probability of violence, the one most thoroughly studied is a gene causing deficiency of monoamine oxidase A (MAOA). After a neuron releases serotonin, dopamine, or norepinephrine, most of it returns to the neuron via reuptake.","A deficiency MAOA increases the build-up of serotonin inside neurons, evidently altering early brain development in a way that increases the risk of antisocial behavior, especially in males.","Because the MAOA gene is on the X chromosome, males are far more likely than females to have the variant form of the gene without a normal form to compete with it.","Research with mice also demonstrates a link between a genetic deficiency of MAOA and later aggressive behavior. This result is fascinating because of its apparent demonstration of an interaction between genetics and environment.","Most fighting in the animal kingdom is by males competing for mates, and their aggressive behavior depends on testosterone.","The natural assumption is that testosterone increases violent behavior, and yet, for humans the evidence is","In those cases, the correlation between baseline testosterone level and aggressive behavior is statistically significant (if we study a large enough group), but low (less than 0.1). The amount that testosterone increases in an emotional situation correlates a little higher with aggression, but still less than 0.2.","Because females start with low testosterone levels, an increase might produce more effect than it does in males.","In one study, testosterone increased the amount of time females spent looking at angry faces. This result fits with other research finding that committees work more harmoniously if they include a high percentage of females—of course, females who hadn’t just been given testosterone.","Several lines of evidence link impulsive, aggressive behavior to low serotonin release.","Luigi Valzelli found that isolating male mice for 4 weeks increased their aggressive behavior and decreased their serotonin turnover, the amount that neurons released and replaced.","When neurons release serotonin, they reabsorb most of it and synthesize enough to replace the amount that washed away.","Researchers measure serotonin turnover by the concentration of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), serotonin’s main metabolite, in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). One reason is that some studies measured actual behavior, whereas others relied on answers to questionnaires.","Also, many studies relied on serotonin measurements from the blood, which correlates poorly with serotonin in the brain.","Overall, low serotonin turnover does appear to correlate with human aggressive behavior, but not strongly.","Cortisol increases during anxiety and decreases during anger. A study of adolescents found aggressive behavior correlated with high levels of testosterone and low levels of cortisol in their hair.","This type of behavior is a long way from serious violence, and maybe that is why most experiments find only weak relationships to testosterone or other chemicals.","Yes, at least one: A sudden loud noise causes newborns to arch their backs, briefly extend their arms and legs, and cry.","Whether to call this behavior fear is a matter of opinion. (The alternative is “distress.”) After infancy, a loud noise elicits the closely related startle reflex: Auditory information from the cochlear nucleus in the medulla goes directly to an area in the pons that tenses the muscles, especially the neck muscles.","Tensing the neck muscles is important because the neck is so vulnerable to injury.","Although you don’t have to learn to fear loud noises, your current mood or situation modifies your reaction. So do people who report much anxiety, even if they don’t qualify for a psychiatric diagnosis.","The suitability of the startle reflex to measure anxiety means that we can use it with not only with humans, but also with laboratory animals to explore the brain mechanisms.","Extensive research with rodents has demonstrated the importance of the amygdala for fear and anxiety.","The brain pathways are the same in humans, but the research can go into more detail with rodents.","In research with rodents, psychologists first measure the startle response to a sudden loud noise.","Conversely, a stimulus previously associated with something pleasant, or with the absence of danger, becomes a safety signal that decreases the startle reflex. Investigators determined that the amygdala (Figures 11.10 and 11.13) is important for modifying the startle reflex, and for learned fears in general.","An odd parasite has evolved a way to exploit the consequences of amygdala damage.","Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan that infects many mammals but reproduces only in cats.","When the parasite enters a rodent, in many cases (about 50 percent) it migrates to the brain where it damages the amygdala. The amygdala is important for learning to fear a particular stimulus, but that is not the only type of fear.","I need to be alert for threats.” This long-term, generalized emotional arousal depends on a brain area called the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis.","The effect of amygdala damage in monkeys was first described in classic studies early in the 1900s and is known as the Klüver-Bucy syndrome, from the names of the primary investigators.","Monkeys with this syndrome are tame and placid.","They attempt to pick up lighted matches and other objects that they ordinarily avoid.","They display less than the normal fear of snakes or dominant monkeys. They have impaired social behaviors, largely because they don’t seem to learn which monkeys to approach with caution.","Like rats with amygdala damage, monkeys with such damage are impaired at learning what to fear.","Studies with fMRI find that the human amygdala responds strongly when people look at photos that arouse fear or at photos of faces expressing fear or anger.","The amygdala can also respond to pleasant stimuli if a task requires attention to pleasant stimuli, but even then, the response is never as great as it is to unpleasant stimuli.","The amygdala’s response to a frightened face emerges in the remarkably fast time of just 74 milliseconds (ms) after presentation of the photo, faster than the response by the fusiform gyrus and other areas responsible for facial recognition.","You respond to the fear in someone’s face before you recognize whose face it is. Contrary to what we might guess, the amygdala responds most strongly when a facial expression is difficult to interpret.","It is usually easy to interpret an angry face looking straight at you, but a fearful face looking straight at you can be puzzling.","With laboratory animals, researchers can intentionally damage the amygdala to see the effects.","When people experience a stroke that damages the amygdala and surrounding areas, at least in one hemisphere, they are impaired in certain ways.","They can classify photos as pleasant versus unpleasant about as well as anyone else, but they experience less arousal from viewing unpleasant pictures. They have no problem with the cognitive aspect of unpleasant emotions, but they lack much of the feeling aspect.","People with the rare genetic Urbach-Wiethe disease accumulate calcium in the amygdala until it wastes away, without much damage to surrounding structures.","Much of the research deals with a woman known by her initials, SM, who describes herself as fearless, and certainly acts that way. When she viewed 10 clips from the scariest movies the researchers could find, she reported feeling only excitement, not fear.","When the researchers took her to a “haunted house,” she led the way without hesitation, venturing down dark hallways. Aggressive behavior in humans correlates with increased testosterone levels and decreased cortisol, but the correlations are weak, partly because of the difficulty of measuring aggressive behavior.","Enhancement of the startle reflex indicates anxiety or learned fears."],"classroomCoverage":{"status":"source_structured_full_book","level":"comprehensive_book_derived","topicHeadings":15,"bullets":61,"newWords":2450,"allTopicsWithExplanations":true,"sourceScope":"verified_pdf_topic_facts_crosschecked_with_uploaded_markdown"},"classroomFigures":[{"id":"figure-11-13","headingId":"bp14-m11-2-h06","number":"11.13","title":"Amygdala and learned fears","printedPage":367,"pdfPage":385,"alt":"Excerpt from Figure 11.13 of Kalat Biological Psychology, showing amygdala and learned fears.","image":"data:image/webp;base64,","width":1016,"height":654,"source":"Cropped figure from user-supplied textbook PDF","cropPdfPoints":[68,62,576,389],"status":"figure number and printed page checked in PDF; crop visually reviewed by montage"}]},{"id":"bp14-m11-3","chapterId":"bp14-ch11","moduleId":"bp14-m11-3","moduleNumber":"11.3","title":"Emotional Reactions to Stress","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":376,"printedEnd":382,"pdfStart":394,"pdfEnd":400,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress influences both emotional experience and bodily function. The general adaptation syndrome and the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis describe important components of the physiological stress response."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The book also considers the immune system, the enteric nervous system, and coping. Follow how a temporary response may differ from the effects of persistent stress."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-3-study-1","text":"Stress as an adaptive response"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress arises when an organism faces demands or threats requiring adjustment. The general adaptation syndrome describes a broad pattern of bodily response that changes over time. In an acute challenge, physiological activation may support attention and action. Prolonged activation, however, can contribute to wear on bodily systems. Whether a particular demand is harmful depends on intensity, duration, resources, and interpretation, not simply the presence of a measurable stress hormone."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-3-study-2","text":"The hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The HPA axis links brain signals to endocrine activity. Hypothalamic signaling influences the pituitary, which in turn influences adrenal cortex secretion of glucocorticoids such as cortisol. This helps organize metabolic and other responses to challenge. Feedback mechanisms regulate the system, and its time course differs from faster autonomic responses. A useful revision skill is to trace the sequence of glands and signals without mixing it up with the sympathetic nervous system."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-3-study-3","text":"Stress and immunity"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Immune processes interact with nervous and endocrine systems. Stress can influence immune activity, and its effects differ across acute versus prolonged circumstances and across immune outcomes. These connections do not mean stress is the sole cause of infection or illness. The enteric nervous system and gut-related communication provide additional routes linking bodily states with behavior. Biological evidence should be interpreted in context rather than reduced to the slogan that stress 'weakens everything'."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-3-study-4","text":"Coping and regulation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Coping strategies can change exposure to a stressor, a person's interpretation, or the bodily consequences of ongoing strain. Social support, controllability, and circumstances matter. The best way to study stress is to connect three levels: the demanding event, the brain–hormone–immune processes it recruits, and the person's behavioral response. Different interventions act at different levels, which is why no single coping technique solves every problem."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h01","text":"Stress and the General Adaptation Syndrome"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hans Selye popularized the concept of stress , defining it as the nonspecific response of the body to any demand made upon it.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Selye inferred that any threat activated a generalized response, which he called the general adaptation syndrome .","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the initial stage, which he called alarm, the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for brief emergency activity.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The anterior pituitary gland secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) , which stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete glucocorticoid hormones, mainly cortisol in humans.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The HPA axis reacts to stress more gradually than the sympathetic nervous system, but its effects continue as long as the stress continues.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After intense, prolonged stress, the body enters the third stage, exhaustion , when the nervous and immune systems no longer have the energy to sustain their responses.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress-related illnesses and psychiatric problems are widespread in industrial societies, possibly because of changes in the type of stresses we face.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Selye’s concept of stress included any change in one’s life, including both favorable and unfavorable events.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Still, as Jerome Kagan observed, researchers’ concepts of stress have ranged from life-threatening events to matters of brief inconvenience.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h02","text":"Stress and the Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Adrenal Cortex Axis"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress can impair health indirectly by altering people’s behaviors.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Widows and widowers have a greatly increased risk of heart attack or stroke for the next several months , largely because they tend to eat worse meals, consume more alcohol, sleep less, and exercise less than previously .","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress also alters nervous system activity in ways that impair health.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brief or moderate stress improves energetic performance, vigilance, and memory formation, especially for learning fears .","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brief stress enhances activity of the immune system, helping it fight illnesses, but prolonged stress impairs immune activity and memory .","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h03","text":"The Immune System"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The immune system consists of cells that protect the body against viruses, bacteria, and other intruders.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The immune system is like a police force: If it is too weak, the criminals (viruses and bacteria) run wild and create damage.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If it becomes too strong, it might start attacking law-abiding citizens (the body’s own cells).","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the immune system attacks normal cells, we call the result an autoimmune","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The primary components of the immune system are the leukocytes , commonly known as white blood .","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A study of research scientists in Antarctica found that a 9-month period of .","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brief or mild levels of stress produces cortisol that puts the brakes on excess drive.","headingId":"bp14-m11-3-h03","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395},{"type":"bullet","text":"Recall Selye’s observation that most illnesses produce similar symptoms, such as fever, loss hippocampus.","headingId":"bp14-m11-3-h04","sourcePrintedPage":379,"sourcePdfPage":397},{"type":"bullet","text":"Much of the variance in how you respond to stress comes from the bacteria in the The general adaptation syndrome describes a broad pattern of bodily response that changes over time. In an acute challenge, physiological activation may support attention and action. Prolonged activation, however, can contribute to wear on bodily systems. Whether a particular demand is harmful depends on intensity, duration, resources, and interpretation, not simply the presence of a measurable stress hormone.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":376,"sourcePrintedEnd":382,"sourcePdfStart":394,"sourcePdfEnd":400},{"id":"bp14-m11-3-study-2","title":"The hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis","text":"The HPA axis links brain signals to endocrine activity. Hypothalamic signaling influences the pituitary, which in turn influences adrenal cortex secretion of glucocorticoids such as cortisol. This helps organize metabolic and other responses to challenge. Feedback mechanisms regulate the system, and its time course differs from faster autonomic responses. A useful revision skill is to trace the sequence of glands and signals without mixing it up with the sympathetic nervous system.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":376,"sourcePrintedEnd":382,"sourcePdfStart":394,"sourcePdfEnd":400},{"id":"bp14-m11-3-study-3","title":"Stress and immunity","text":"Immune processes interact with nervous and endocrine systems. Stress can influence immune activity, and its effects differ across acute versus prolonged circumstances and across immune outcomes. These connections do not mean stress is the sole cause of infection or illness. The enteric nervous system and gut-related communication provide additional routes linking bodily states with behavior. Biological evidence should be interpreted in context rather than reduced to the slogan that stress 'weakens everything'.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":376,"sourcePrintedEnd":382,"sourcePdfStart":394,"sourcePdfEnd":400},{"id":"bp14-m11-3-study-4","title":"Coping and regulation","text":"Coping strategies can change exposure to a stressor, a person's interpretation, or the bodily consequences of ongoing strain. As predicted, the brain responses corresponded to people’s self-reports that social support from a loved one helps reduce stress.","paragraphIndex":20032,"printedPages":[379]},{"label":"Additional explanation","explanation":"The organization in the best position to do such a study is the military.","paragraphIndex":20033,"printedPages":[379]}],"status":"whole_book_source_structured_classroom_notes","basis":"uploaded_textbook_pdf_and_markdown","evidenceMethod":"source_heading_facts","sourceFactCount":6,"editorialVerification":"source-aligned, individual paraphrase review pending","followUpExplanation":"We now see why: The body reacts to prolonged stress by activating the adrenal cortex and the immune system, and the resulting increase in","followUpParagraphIndex":20030}],"classroomParagraphs":["Hans Selye popularized the concept of stress, defining it as the nonspecific response of the body to any demand made upon it.","Selye inferred that any threat activated a generalized response, which he called the general adaptation syndrome.","In the initial stage, which he called alarm, the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for brief emergency activity.","The anterior pituitary gland secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete glucocorticoid hormones, mainly cortisol in humans. The HPA axis reacts to stress more gradually than the sympathetic nervous system, but its effects continue as long as the stress continues.","After intense, prolonged stress, the body enters the third stage, exhaustion, when the nervous and immune systems no longer have the energy to sustain their responses.","Stress-related illnesses and psychiatric problems are widespread in industrial societies, possibly because of changes in the type of stresses we face. Selye’s concept of stress included any change in one’s life, including both favorable and unfavorable events.","Still, as Jerome Kagan observed, researchers’ concepts of stress have ranged from life-threatening events to matters of brief inconvenience.","Stress can impair health indirectly by altering people’s behaviors.","Widows and widowers have a greatly increased risk of heart attack or stroke for the next several months, largely because they tend to eat worse meals, consume more alcohol, sleep less, and exercise less than previously.","Stress also alters nervous system activity in ways that impair health. Brief or moderate stress improves energetic performance, vigilance, and memory formation, especially for learning fears.","Brief stress enhances activity of the immune system, helping it fight illnesses, but prolonged stress impairs immune activity and memory.","The immune system consists of cells that protect the body against viruses, bacteria, and other intruders.","The immune system is like a police force: If it is too weak, the criminals (viruses and bacteria) run wild and create damage.","If it becomes too strong, it might start attacking law-abiding citizens (the body’s own cells). When the immune system attacks normal cells, we call the result an autoimmune","The primary components of the immune system are the leukocytes, commonly known as white blood cells.","In response to an infection, leukocytes and other cells produce small proteins called cytokines (e.g., interleukin-1, or IL-1) that combat infections.","Cytokines fight the illness, but when cytokine levels get too high, they produce nasal congestion, a runny nose, and other symptoms associated with illness. Sleep and inactivity conserve energy so that the body can devote more energy to its immune attack against the intruders.","The nervous system has more control than we might have guessed over the immune system.","The study of this relationship, called psychoneuroimmunology, deals with how experiences alter the immune system and how the immune system in turn influences the central nervous system.","In response to a brief stressful experience, the nervous system activates the immune system to produce more natural killer cells and cytokines. The cytokines help combat infections that might result from an injury, and they also trigger prostaglandins that reach the hypothalamus, where they produce the same effects as an illness—sleepiness, decreased appetite, and elevated body temperature.","Even viewing extremely disgusting images can activate the immune system and raise body temperature.","A prolonged stress response produces symptoms of depression and weakens the immune system.","A study of research scientists in Antarctica found that a 9-month period of cold, darkness, and social isolation reduced T cell functioning to about half of normal levels. Brief or mild levels of stress produces cortisol that puts the brakes on excess cytokines that produce symptoms of illness, but after prolonged stress, the body becomes less responsive to cortisol and the inflammation continues unabated.","When you experience stress, you notice stomach churning, diarrhea, and other signs of digestive upset.","These are products of the enteric nervous system, a set of neurons that control digestion, stretching from the esophagus to the rectum.","The enteric system reacts to stress because of input from the brain and from the hormones released by stress. Most of those bacteria are helpful, but some produce irritable bowel syndrome and visceral pain, and some produce chemicals that increase the risk of anxiety and depression.","Your reaction to stress depends on what happens throughout your body, not just what happens in your brain.","Coping with stress involves both physiological regulation and social or behavioral resources. Although stress reactions can help in an immediate challenge, prolonged stress may impair health, memory, and flexible behavior.","People with reliable social relationships often show lower distress. In a study discussed by Kalat, holding a spouse’s hand during painful stimulation reduced neural responses in several brain regions.","Decades ago, Hans Selye argued that any stressful event leads to the general adaptation syndrome, marked by fever and other signs of illness.","We now see why: The body reacts to prolonged stress by activating the adrenal cortex and the immune system, and the resulting increase in","Those factors in turn correlate with the ability to rapidly activate the stress response and then rapidly deactivate it.","Holding the husband’s hand reduced the response indicated by fMRI in several brain areas, including the prefrontal cortex. As predicted, the brain responses corresponded to people’s self-reports that social support from a loved one helps reduce stress.","The organization in the best position to do such a study is the military.","Kalat emphasizes social support and resilience. These findings do not imply that one technique removes stress; they show that stress responses vary with relationships, past experiences, and the situation.","Research following people through stressful experiences links greater distress to factors such as earlier trauma, concussions, mental-health difficulties, and limited close social relationships.","Stress has biological effects as well as psychological meanings. Coping strategies can change exposure to stressors or the degree of support available during them.","Sustained stress-related hormonal activity can affect the hippocampus and other bodily systems. Research on the engram has changed over time, and psychologists distinguish working, short-term, and long-term memory."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The module also examines consolidation, Alzheimer’s disease, and infant amnesia. Separate the loss of stored information from difficulty creating or accessing memories when comparing examples of memory impairment."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-1-study-1","text":"Memory is not one storage box"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Learning can change behavior, but memory includes several kinds of information and different neural processes. Short-term retention, working memory, and long-term remembering differ in duration and functional demands. Working memory involves actively maintaining and using information for a current task. Long-term memory includes different forms, such as recalling events or gradually acquiring skills. The possibility that someone can lose one kind of memory while retaining another shows why the word 'memory' should not be treated as a single ability."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-1-study-2","text":"The search for where memories are stored"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Early researchers, including Lashley, investigated whether memories occupy sharply localized brain sites. Results challenged the view that one tiny cortical location contains an entire learned response. Modern approaches investigate distributed neuronal populations and the ways training changes their connectivity. An engram refers to the physical changes underlying a memory, but identifying neurons active during learning is not by itself proof that they constitute the whole memory. Representations may involve several brain regions and time-dependent changes."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-1-study-3","text":"Consolidation and forgetting"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Memories can change after initial learning through consolidation, retrieval, and reconsolidation-related processes. This means the formation of a lasting memory is not simply a one-time filing operation. Forgetting can arise through different mechanisms, including disrupted acquisition, storage, or retrieval. Stress, context, and brain damage may affect these processes differently. When interpreting a memory test, ask what type of learning was required and whether the person could express the information in another way."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-1-study-4","text":"Clinical patterns"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Alzheimer's disease is associated with progressive changes in cognitive function and neural pathology, but memory difficulties alone do not establish that diagnosis. Infant amnesia refers to the limited ability adults have to recall early childhood autobiographical episodes; it does not mean infants are incapable of learning. Such examples demonstrate that memory is constrained by brain development, neural health, and the kind of information being assessed."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h01","text":"Localized one.","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h03","text":"The Modern Search for the cases.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, the time needed to form a long-term memory varies center and a UCS center in the brain that lets excitation of the CS center flow to the UCS center, evoking a response just like the unconditioned response.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404},{"type":"bullet","text":"Regardless, Lashley’s results shared that at least some types of learning did not depend on connections across the cortex.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404},{"type":"bullet","text":"Note, however, another interpretation of Lashley’s results: Maze learning and visual discrimination learning are complex tasks in which a rat attends to visual and tactile stimuli, the location of its body, the position of its head, and other cues.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"At first, a rabbit closed its eye in response to the air puff but not the tone.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"Damaging any of those areas will impair or eliminate the learned response, but we cannot be sure that learning occurred in the damaged area.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"Damage in E or F will prevent learning by blocking the output from D.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"If so, then D has to be active at the time of the learning, and so do the areas leading up to D (A, B, and C).","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"You can repeat something you just heard, and you can also describe something you experienced years ago.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406},{"type":"bullet","text":"Hebb could not imagine a physical or chemical process that is fast enough to account for immediate memory yet stable enough for permanent memory.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406},{"type":"bullet","text":"When you watch a soccer or hockey match, you remember the score until it changes.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you park your car, your memory of its location is neither a short-term memory that fades within seconds, nor a memory that will last for years.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"Flashbulb memories have a further aspect: Suppose you are driving on snow and you skid on a slippery patch.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"Now you form a long-term memory of not only the accident but also the earlier slip.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"You continue staring at the central point until you hear a beep, and then you are supposed to look to where you remember seeing the light.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"Ordinarily, the brain’s representation of a visual image decays quickly, but if you need to remember the stimulus to respond to it later, activity in the visual cortex persists.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"You want to remember where you are supposed to go at 11 o’clock tomorrow morning, and you don’t want to confuse that information with your appointment at 9 o’clock three weeks ago.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"Sometimes amnesia is limited to a certain aspect of memory.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"Here we briefly consider Alzheimer’s disease and the phenomenon of infant amnesia.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"The second module considers amnesia resulting from damage to the hippocampus.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"Daniel Schacter (1983) reported playing golf with an Alzheimer’s patient who remembered the rules and jargon of the game correctly but kept forgetting how many strokes he took.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"People with one copy of the type 4 gene ( APOE4 ) have four times the normal risk of Alzheimer’s, and people with two copies have 15 times the normal risk.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"They also damage axons and dendrites, causing them to cluster into structures called plaques, as Figures 12.6 and 12.7 show.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":391,"sourcePdfPage":409},{"type":"bullet","text":"Many old people have high levels of b -amyloid without Alzheimer’s disease, and some have Alzheimer’s disease without especially high levels of b -amyloid.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":391,"sourcePdfPage":409},{"type":"bullet","text":"Pharmaceutical companies have made many attempts to alleviate Alzheimer’s by drugs that counteract b -amyloid, without much success.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Another explanation for the ineffectiveness of drugs so far is that the damage associated with Alzheimer’s may already be too extensive by the time the condition is diagnosed.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Later psychologists have offered explanations of why young children fail to form long-term memories, but in fact young children do form long-term memories.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h10","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Decades ago, Karl Lashley supposed that the physiology of learning might be a simple matter of increasing a single pathway in the cortex.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h11","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Hypotheses have included the development of language, or a sense of self, or complex reasoning abilities as children grow older.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h11","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Rats in their first weeks of life learn and retain their learning for a day or more, but they soon forget.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h11","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Lashley sought to find the engram, the physiological representation of learning.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h11","sourcePrintedPage":393,"sourcePdfPage":411},{"type":"bullet","text":"Donald Hebb reasoned that no one mechanism could account for all the phenomena of learning.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406},{"type":"bullet","text":"First, many short-term memories are not simply on their way to being long-term memories.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"Hitch introduced the term working memory to refer to the way we store information while we are working with it.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407}],"topicIds":["bp14-m12-1-h01","bp14-m12-1-h02","bp14-m12-1-h03","bp14-m12-1-h04","bp14-m12-1-h05","bp14-m12-1-h06","bp14-m12-1-h07","bp14-m12-1-h08","bp14-m12-1-h09","bp14-m12-1-h10","bp14-m12-1-h11"],"studySections":[{"id":"bp14-m12-1-study-1","title":"Memory is not one storage box","text":"Learning can change behavior, but memory includes several kinds of information and different neural processes. Short-term retention, working memory, and long-term remembering differ in duration and functional demands. Working memory involves actively maintaining and using information for a current task. Long-term memory includes different forms, such as recalling events or gradually acquiring skills. The possibility that someone can lose one kind of memory while retaining another shows why the word 'memory' should not be treated as a single ability.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":384,"sourcePrintedEnd":394,"sourcePdfStart":402,"sourcePdfEnd":412},{"id":"bp14-m12-1-study-2","title":"The search for where memories are stored","text":"Early researchers, including Lashley, investigated whether memories occupy sharply localized brain sites. Results challenged the view that one tiny cortical location contains an entire learned response. Modern approaches investigate distributed neuronal populations and the ways training changes their connectivity. An engram refers to the physical changes underlying a memory, but identifying neurons active during learning is not by itself proof that they constitute the whole memory. Representations may involve several brain regions and time-dependent changes.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":384,"sourcePrintedEnd":394,"sourcePdfStart":402,"sourcePdfEnd":412},{"id":"bp14-m12-1-study-3","title":"Consolidation and forgetting","text":"Memories can change after initial learning through consolidation, retrieval, and reconsolidation-related processes. This means the formation of a lasting memory is not simply a one-time filing operation. Forgetting can arise through different mechanisms, including disrupted acquisition, storage, or retrieval. Stress, context, and brain damage may affect these processes differently. When interpreting a memory test, ask what type of learning was required and whether the person could express the information in another way.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":384,"sourcePrintedEnd":394,"sourcePdfStart":402,"sourcePdfEnd":412},{"id":"bp14-m12-1-study-4","title":"Clinical patterns","text":"Alzheimer's disease is associated with progressive changes in cognitive function and neural pathology, but memory difficulties alone do not establish that diagnosis. Infant amnesia refers to the limited ability adults have to recall early childhood autobiographical episodes; it does not mean infants are incapable of learning. Such examples demonstrate that memory is constrained by brain development, neural health, and the kind of information being assessed.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":384,"sourcePrintedEnd":394,"sourcePdfStart":402,"sourcePdfEnd":412}],"contentLevel":"complete_sample_classroom_notes_plus_legacy_source_extraction","selfCheck":[{"question":"Can you explain: Memory is not one storage box?","answer":"Learning can change behavior, but memory includes several kinds of information and different neural processes. between two brain areas would be a possible example of an engram.","printedPage":386,"pdfPage":404,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":21},{"text":"Lashley reasoned that if learning depends on new or theory.","printedPage":386,"pdfPage":404,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":23},{"text":"Lashley also tested whether any portion of the cerebral cortex is more important than others for learning.","printedPage":386,"pdfPage":404,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":24},{"text":"Eventually, researchers
